bp: This paper studies a quiet but powerful decision inside Amazon: whether a product page gets a featured buying slot at all. The Buy Box is the ordinary button area through which almost all Amazon sales flow. When it is present, a shopper can quickly buy from the seller Amazon chooses to feature. When it is suppressed, no offer is featured, even though sellers may still be listing the product. That matters because a platform rule that looks like page design can become market governance. It can decide which sellers are visible, which ads can run, and whether buyers find a product through search. The paper asks what makes Amazon remove this slot and what happens afterward. The real object is not a recommendation model or a price formula. It is a marketplace gate that controls attention, sales opportunity, and seller dependence on one platform-owned path to purchase.
wh: The difficulty is that suppression is both frequent enough to matter and hidden enough to be hard to study. Amazon does not publish a simple public rule saying exactly when the Buy Box disappears. A product can have many sellers, prices can change hour by hour, and competitor offers outside Amazon can move at the same time. If suppression follows a price drop somewhere else, one might think Amazon is disciplining sellers to keep prices aligned across marketplaces. If suppression follows changes to offers on Amazon itself, the story is more about the platform reacting to its own marketplace conditions. These explanations look similar unless the observer sees the timing very closely. A weekly snapshot would miss the order of events. Even daily data could confuse cause and aftermath. The researchers therefore need a high-frequency record of product pages, Amazon offers, outside competitor offers, search position, ad placement, and sales rank over time.
naive: A smart beginner would take a list of suppressed products, compare their prices with competitor prices, and look for a simple rule: suppress when Amazon is not cheapest, or suppress when a seller raises a price. That fails because suppression is an event in time, not just a product property. The price seen after suppression may not be the price that triggered it. A product can also change in several ways at once: sellers enter or leave, offers shift, and competitors update prices. A single before-and-after comparison would mix the trigger with the consequences. It would also miss fast effects such as ads disappearing within 12 hours or search visibility falling immediately.
ap: The central move is to turn platform governance into an observable time series. The authors build a new dataset that watches 17,754 Amazon products every hour for eight weeks in 2024 and pairs those observations with offers from 59,301 unique competitors. Instead of treating suppression as a mystery label attached to a product, they watch the Buy Box appear or disappear while nearby marketplace facts change. That lets them ask a concrete timing question: what changed just before suppression became visible? The answer in the abstract is that changes to offers on Amazon are the primary reason. Lower competitor prices only modestly raise the chance of suppression. The same time record then becomes an impact study. After suppression, products fall sharply in search, ad placements disappear within 12 hours, and sales ranks are 12 percent worse after 48 hours.
mech: The mechanism starts with a set of product pages on Amazon and a repeated clock. At each hourly tick, the collection system records whether the product has a Buy Box or whether the Buy Box is suppressed. Around that same moment, it records offers connected to the product on Amazon and corresponding offers from competitors. The input is therefore not one table of products, but a moving record: product by product, hour by hour, with the page state and the surrounding offers kept together. First, the researchers identify moments when the page moves into suppression. Second, they compare those moments with recent changes in the offers on Amazon and with lower competitor prices outside Amazon. Third, they estimate which observed changes are associated with a higher probability that suppression occurs. Fourth, they examine what happens after suppression by following search position, ad placement, and sales rank on later hourly records. The output has two parts. One part is a determinants account: Amazon-offer changes appear to explain suppression more than lower outside prices do. The other part is an effects account: once the Buy Box is gone, product visibility drops quickly, ads vanish within 12 hours, and sales rank worsens after 48 hours.
math: The main mathematical idea is event comparison over time. In plain terms, the researchers need to ask whether one kind of change tends to happen before another event more often than chance or background movement would suggest. The event is Buy Box suppression. The possible signals are changes to offers on Amazon and lower prices from competitors. Probability enters because the result is not a claim that every single suppression has the same cause. It is a measured chance: when certain offer conditions are observed, how much does the likelihood of suppression change? Time matters because a cause should appear before the event, while an effect should appear after it. Ranking also matters, but in a different way. Search position and sales rank are ordered lists, so the harm is measured partly by movement downward in an order that controls attention. The mathematical tradeoff is close observation versus broad proof. Hourly data helps separate triggers from consequences, but the abstract does not claim a randomized experiment. The math can show strong timing patterns and measured associations; it cannot by itself prove every hidden platform rule.
dots: This paper belongs to the repo's advertising and e-commerce family because it treats commerce as allocation under partial evidence: a platform decides which offer, ad, or page element gets scarce shopper attention. It also connects to the ranking concept, since suppression affects where a product sits in search and whether it can appear in ad placements. The paper is adjacent to marketplace evaluation work because it asks whether platform outcomes should be measured only by buyer convenience or also by seller visibility, advertising access, and competition. It also connects to probability because the study estimates which observed conditions raise the chance of suppression rather than claiming one visible rule explains every case. Compared with papers that improve product ranking or ad targeting, this one studies the governance layer underneath them. Before a seller can benefit from ranking, recommendation, or advertising, the platform may first decide whether the central buying slot exists.
ww: The approach works because the important clues are in the order of events. If the researchers only knew which products were suppressed at some point during eight weeks, they would have to guess whether competitor prices, Amazon-offer changes, search drops, and ad disappearance were causes or consequences. Hourly tracking shrinks that ambiguity. When a Buy Box disappears shortly after changes to offers on Amazon, and lower competitor prices have only a modest relationship with suppression, the platform-governance story becomes more precise. The method also works because it follows several downstream channels rather than treating seller harm as an abstract possibility. Search, ads, and sales rank are different pathways by which shoppers reach products. Seeing search fall immediately, ad placements disappear within 12 hours, and rank worsen after 48 hours shows that suppression is not just a cosmetic page state. It changes the routes through which demand reaches sellers. That is stronger than merely saying sellers might be hurt.
po: The payoff is a clearer account of a marketplace control that was underexplored despite shaping most Amazon sales. The paper provides a high-frequency dataset and open-source collection code, so other researchers can inspect suppression rather than relying only on anecdotes or static screenshots. Substantively, it finds that suppression is driven primarily by changes to offers on Amazon, while lower competitor prices have only a modest effect. It also measures seller-facing consequences: sharp search decline, complete loss of ad placements within 12 hours, and 12 percent worse sales ranks after 48 hours. The abstract finds no short-run competitor-price impact.
limits: The evidence is strong for the observed products, period, and measures, but it is not unlimited. The dataset covers 17,754 products over eight weeks in 2024, so rules could differ across categories, seasons, countries, or later platform changes. The abstract reports timing and probability patterns, not direct access to Amazon's internal decision rule. That means the study can infer determinants from observed events, but it cannot prove the private logic used for every suppression. The short-run finding on competitor prices also leaves longer-run competitive effects unresolved. Finally, seller harm is measured through visibility, ads, and sales rank, not full profit, inventory, or business survival.
